content: Feedback and audit tools are a collection of interconnected quality improvement instruments designed to periodically evaluate adherence to the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) and Selected Practice Recommendations (SPR) guidelines. These tools include the Provider Survey, the Contraceptive Method Mix Assessment, and the Measuring Adherence to Guidance Tool, which is used to monitor progress. The implementation of these tools is not a static process. As the MEC/SPR guidelines are introduced, updated, or adapted for specific settings, it is essential to monitor this process and provide feedback to healthcare providers, clinics, and programs. The data obtained from these assessments can be utilized to implement targeted interventions, such as individual coaching, training, technical assistance, or programmatic and policy changes. The Provider Survey is a tool that can be used to identify knowledge or practice gaps among clinical providers. It can be conducted periodically and may be administered anonymously to assess overall practices or linked to individual providers to identify specific coaching or training needs. The accompanying Interpretation Guide highlights the key concepts being evaluated and connects them to the MEC/SPR guidelines. Depending on the size and culture of the clinical setting, the survey can be tailored to fit the needs of the environment. The Contraceptive Method Mix Assessment Tool is designed to periodically monitor the distribution of contraceptive methods that clients are actually receiving. Local implementation teams or clinic managers can use this tool to evaluate the mix of contraceptive methods and identify potential gaps. Incorporating fidelity metrics from the Measuring Adherence to Guidance Tool can help track the successful integration of WHO’s family planning guidelines into national family planning guidance documents. The Provider Survey of Family Planning Practices includes several components. Part I focuses on demographics, while Part II assesses contraceptive method availability. Part III evaluates provider practices. Questions 1-4 in the demographics section are informational only. If questions 5-6 reveal that many providers have not been trained on a specific method, formal training may be necessary. If methods are unavailable or limited throughout the clinic, management should investigate the reasons for these limitations. Once surveys and assessments are completed, it may not always be clear what is causing gaps in care. To uncover root causes, it is critical to conduct investigations in a culture of improvement rather than punishment. Examples of strategies include group meetings to discuss results and explore solutions, direct observation of clinic practices and provider-client interactions, or using an external observer acting as a client to report on their experience (mystery clients). The Implementation Guide Toolkit provides a structured approach to addressing gaps. It includes steps such as identifying relevant client groups for assessment, monitoring and reassessing practices, and exploring barriers at the client, provider, or clinic level. For example, if the contraceptive method mix is skewed, it is important to investigate whether all methods are available, whether there are supply chain issues, or whether external factors are influencing these outcomes. The Measuring Adherence to Guidance Tool is used to monitor the successful implementation of WHO’s family planning guidelines at the national, facility, and provider levels. This involves setting targets based on metrics relevant to the specific setting, developing strategies and processes to collect data, and carefully timing assessments for certain indicators. Data collection and recording outcomes at each level are essential steps in this process.
